summary.text:
A tidy book with one dated event in it. Westmorland & Furness holds £176.279m at 3.70% over an average 22.6 years against a CFR of £275.249m, leaving £98.970m internal with other long-term liabilities at nil. Our holding of their PWLB loans matches exactly once their £13,000,000 FMS Wertmanagement market loan is taken out: 27 loans, £163,278,734, against a schedule total of £176,278,734.

The event is a single loan. The 8.5% sitting under twelve months in their maturity indicator is £14,000,000 of PWLB at 4.50%, taken on 14 November 2001 and maturing 13 November 2026 — three months after this report went to Council, and the only debt event inside the year. Behind it sits genuinely cheap long money: £55m at 2.16% to 2.32% running to 2063, 2067 and 2068.

The pressure is the cash. Balances halved over the year, from £140.9m to £74.6m, while the internal position stands at £98.970m — so the borrowing being suppressed is now larger than the cash suppressing it. The treasury underspend of £6.300m splits exactly into £3.291m from taking no new external borrowing and £3.009m of interest above budget, which is a neat illustration of how much of the saving depends on holding cash. No officer address is published in the appendix.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the capital programme and treasury outturn report that went to Full Council on 30 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 27 PWLB loans for Westmorland and Furness totalling £163,278,734, which sits inside the £173.6m debt portfolio in your paragraph 3.34, the balance being non-PWLB.

Paragraph 3.32 is the interesting one: no new external borrowing at all in the year, with previously approved borrowing run against short-term cash reserves instead. Paragraph 3.34 then gives both halves of what that trade earned — £74.6m of temporary investments at 4.07% against a debt portfolio costing 3.7%. So the cash was earning more than the debt cost, and the loans that would have funded the capital programme were never drawn. It shows up as a one-off £3.291m saving inside a £14.650m treasury budget and a £6.300m provisional underspend.

That is a position with a shelf life, which is the only reason we mention it. It works while short rates sit above the average cost of your book, and it stops working when they don't. Bank Rate is 3.75% and one-year PWLB certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26, so it is still working comfortably today. The forward curve is the thing that tells you when the arithmetic turns, and we publish the implied Bank Rate path from SONIA daily rather than quarterly.

The other half is the deferred borrowing itself. Your capital programme has moved from £432.130m as approved in February 2025 to £591.108m at outturn, with £65.139m of that agreed at February 2026 Council alone. Both of your build-up tables foot exactly, which we checked. At some point that spend meets the borrowing decision this strategy is postponing, and the price on that day is what matters. July's sector borrowing was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — a thin month, which is worth knowing before you need to be in it. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One thing from our own data, offered because it is not in your covering report. Running your 27 loans through the DMO's premature repayment formula on this afternoon's curve, twenty-six of them price below par — about £38.7m of discount against a £163.3m balance, with roughly £28.6m of it in three loans: the £25m at 2.32% to 2067, the £20m at 2.16% to 2063 and the £10m at 2.25% to 2068. We are not suggesting anything follows. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote — ours is indicative and the page says so. It is simply a number that exists and moves, and it is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit. Liability Benchmark: the essentials, which is the indicator that answers "how long can we keep not borrowing" and is exactly the question your strategy turns on. Cash-flow forecasting & daily cash next to it. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator for the position above. And Devolution & reorganisation: the treasury view, which we have found lands well with authorities still carrying predecessor structures. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Capital Programme Update & Treasury Management 2025/26 Outturn Report, Full Council, 30 July 2026 (treasury outturn to Cabinet, 14 July 2026).
